speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has taken us some time to reach this very important item under which assistance will be given to the farmers in the Peace River area. It is the first item in these estimates. In speaking this afternoon in committee, I want to say that following correspondence and telephone calls which I have received, I am very concerned about the amount of assistance that has been offered to farmers in the Peace River country, both in Alberta and in British Columbia. This Committee should be made aware of the fact that their need is very great and that it has not been met by the amounts of money that have been provided for the relief of these farmers. Possibly the first move has properly been made in providing a blanket solution. However, on examining the situation closely I find that the farmers in various parts of the Peace River region have not suffered these hardships equally. There are areas which have suffered a total loss, while in others significant amounts of the crop have been recovered.
In addition to what has been done, I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) himself make a detailed on-the-spot survey of the conditions that exist in that part of the prairie region. My understanding is that he has been in Edmonton, met with ministers of the Alberta and British Columbia governments, and received reports from them. I say he should go personally to that area, talk to the farm families, and find out how those people are making out. I hope he will do this.
I hold in my hand an article from the Globe and Mail, a Toronto paper. It is headed, "A White Disaster for Peace River." It describes the real hardships that exist in certain parts of the Peace River country. I say that the minister should see to it that the people there receive all necessary assistance from other Canadians. This article in the Globe and Mail reports that farm families in the area say that what has been done to date is not adequate.
I also have a letter here from one of the Farm Union representatives in the Peace River area. He writes that there will be real hardship unless a more adequate and comprehensive job is done. I quote from his letter as follows:
In short, the farm economy here requires a substantial injection of capital if it is to remain viable. Nothing less will guarantee its continuation as a contributor to the welfare of the country. I would suggest that the government has already set this sort of precedent. It has found it advisable, or expedient, to inject great amounts of cash into any number of projects of no more importance than this-OFY programs, manpower training programs, DREE incentive grants, and not the least, great tax concessions to any number and variety of corporations, many of them foreign owned.
We have provided assistance for corporations already. When the United States proposed, and indeed imposed, restrictions against the export of certain Canadian manufactured goods to the United States, we took action not more than a year ago to provide assistance. And we did
Supply
not make it a limited program. We made it an open-ended program so that if companies could prove the damage done to them and the amount they needed, that amount of money would be paid under the formula in the act that we passed. I, as a farmer, as a Prairie representative, voted for that legislation. I, and others on this side of the House, thought it was necessary to keep Canadians in business. We did not think that Canadian businesses should be destroyed. All I am pleading this afternoon is that we do as much for the people who suffered disaster in western Canada as we were prepared to do for corporations in eastern Canada. I do not know if the Minister of Agriculture will pay any attention to my plea. I had hoped he would be in the House this afternoon when we were discussing estimates which affect his department. Perhaps he did not receive enough notice; I do not know, but I hope he will read the reports of the speeches made by those who are talking on behalf of these farmers.
These particular farmers suffered difficulties in previous years. That is why they are in straightened circumstances. Their reserves of credit and cash were already badly depleted. I understand that in that area the Farm Credit Corporation is not pressing collections on money owed to it. I say that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board should make representations to that board not to press collections under its cash advances program, in instances where farmers, because of weather conditions, have been unable to deliver grain and will not be able to deliver grain. There is no point in harassing those people at this time because they have neither grain nor money. The old saying that you cannot get blood out of a turnip is still true. I urge that minister to consult with officials of the Wheat Board to see if some assistance can be given in that area. Of course, interest rates have been a factor in the whole equation, but not the only one.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture did give some undertaking at a meeting of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee, when I asked him if the government would give consideration to providing supplies of seed grain so that farmers could put in another crop in this area. He replied:
We will be watching it very closely. If our investigations show that there may be a need to move jointly in seeds, etc., for them, we will do it. We already know the plans that we made on shipping feed in for the livestock and again there is not going to be the need that we thought there was for this unless it speeds up tremendously.
I call the attention of the House to that commitment, and hope adequate funds will be provided so that farmers can put in another crop and take it off properly.
Now, I wish to speak briefly about the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. Additional money is provided in these supplementary estimates for the transportation of feed grains. Again, I understand that this need arises in part because of bad weather conditions in eastern Canada, which resulted in less production of grain and corn than had been expected. As a result, we find it necessary to move larger amounts of feed grain into eastern regions to meet the needs of farmers there. I want to say that as far as we are concerned, we are prepared to see these amounts come before this committee, and we are prepared to support them so that farmers will be assured of the amounts of grain that they need. We are always pre-
25789-4)

Supply
pared to see a fair and workable agricultural arrangement between the various regions of Canada.
I want to say, too, Mr. Chairman, that we are concerned about the Wheat Board's handling of grain, particularly about the present situation that exists in western Canada and most particularly in the province of Saskatchewan and in my constituency, in regard to the marketing of rapeseed. I am informed that some farmers are delivering rapeseed under contract for less than the current market price. At some points in my constituency grain companies are paying 30 cents to 35 cents a bushel more than at other points in the same constituency. Places like Kinley, where the higher prices are paid, are plugged and farmers at that point are not able to deliver the quantities of wheat that they should under their quota because other farmers 50 or 60 miles east are delivering grain so that they can get the Vancouver price.
Two or three years ago I said to the then minister in charge of the Wheat Board that two future markets operating in western Canada could only work to the disadvantage of the western farmer, and this is what has happened. The only reasonable solution to the problem is to bring these other non-board grains under the Canadian Wheat Board and have an efficient method of marketing and pricing. The quota regulations are working to the disadvantage of the ordinary producers of rapeseed because of the present price situation and an explanation is owed to them. They should not have to spend their time in a truck taking their grain to another area in order to get the higher price; it should be available to them at their own elevator door. Perhaps the minister can clear up this problem when he speaks about the production and marketing of feed grains.
The price of rapeseed and the method of marketing will have a very important effect on planting programs in the coming year. The method of pricing barley will also have a profound effect on the plans of farmers in the coming year. There is nothing in the actions of the government to suggest that they have given any serious consideration to these factors. The minister makes vague noises now and then about bringing other grains under the Wheat Board, but in the last parliament when he and his party had a chance to do this they voted against it. When the Conservatives had a chance to do it, they also voted against it.
It would be interesting, Mr. Chairman, if the Conservatives would state their policy in regard to marketing. Do they want a free-wheeling, open market for feed grains and rapeseed across Canada or do they want them marketed through the Wheat Board, giving a fair deal to those who buy and those who sell? I am offering the Conservatives the same challenge on grain marketing that my leader offered them on the pension program half an hour ago. When are they going to stand up and be counted? I will put the policy of our party on the line. We will not continue to put up with the present policies in regard to rapeseed which set producer against producer and farmer against farmer to the advantage of that group who handles it and skims off the profit as the farmer moves it from the field to the marketplace.

We will have a chance to talk on the method of movement of grain later as these estimates move through the Committee, but at this point I should like to deal again with the needs of the men and women and their families in the Peace River country. We need to do more for them because we should not see hardship visited on farm families in Canada without protest. As a final word, Mr. Chairman, I say again to the Minister of Agriculture that he should review his position. He should personally walk with those farmers in their fields and talk to them. After he has done that, he is entitled to make his decision and bring it before the House. He should come here and tell the House what he has seen, then make recommendations on what should be done to meet the situation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to say a few words on the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
I attentively listened a while ago to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) who spoke about agriculture. That member is surely well versed in agriculture, but as many others he does not know all solutions to farming problems.
The hon. member stated that we should find means to stimulate production in Canada, but I wonder whether it would now be advisable to stimulate farming production. Not so long ago, various ways were found to prevent farmers from producing apparently because there were surpluses. Eastern farmers were penalized because they were producing too much while western farmers were paid to prevent them from sowing.
Now, we are told that agriculture has to be invigorated and this, after it has been restricted and mismanaged to a point that about 50 per cent of our farmers are giving it up. A new policy of incentives for agriculture is now being advocated. But I do not think that agriculture can be stimulated with the means we have now. In fact, when a farmer needs machinery, he pays a lot for it, what with taxes and transportation. He also has to pay a very high rate of interest to finance companies when purchasing his implements.
But farmers do need other things besides machinery, like materials, buildings and decent homes. And when purchasing building materials, they must pay an 11 per cent tax just like any other citizen.
And yet we want the price of farm products to go down because the cost of living is too high, and we are seeking ways of bringing it down. Well, bringing the cost of living down for the farmers is a simple matter of removing taxes, bringing down interest rates and granting compensated discounts on products. In fact, the primary incitement for farmers is to enable them to sell their products, which is only possible if citizens have adequate purchasing power.
Now the cost of food is so high that many families are denying themselves necessary food products. I shall give milk as an example: some families could use four or five quarts a day but use only one because they cannot afford to buy more. The government should therefore find a

system for granting compensated discounts in order to bring prices down. By so doing, and through other means, such as reducing interest rates and eliminating taxes on building materials for farmers, we could contribute to bringing down the price of food.
If we brought those prices down, the farmer could sell more products and be less dependent on foreign markets, as other producers in our economy would be. We are seeking all kinds of ways of exporting our products while doing everything to prevent Canadians from purchasing more by burdening them with taxes and excessive interest rates.
Mr. Chairman, how can we find real solutions to this problem when we act in an unthinkable way, against all sense? Common sense requires to reduce interest rates and enable our citizens to buy more by pushing prices down. Yet prices are going up in every field, including that of grain movement; this is the reason why farmers have become unable to make both ends meet and they have gone deeply into debt.
This is why they borrow money. Interest rates, one could argue, are reasonable, but a rate of 8 or 9 per cent is too high for a farmer. It should not exceed 3 per cent.
We shall never settle problems related to agriculture by taking all kinds of measures designed to increase the prices of products; we should rather find other means in order to reduce them.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Crowfoot said that Canadian farm production is not balanced with the U.S. production. He stated that we are unable to produce as cheaply as the Americans do, that there is a difference between prices of American and Canadian products. The American legislation is a little more helpful, a little more human than the Canadian legislation in the area of agriculture. I met some U.S. farmers who borrow all the capital they need at an interest rate of 5 per cent; those American farmers do not pay any tax as long as they work on their farm. This is a system which does not exist in Canada, where farmers must pay taxes just as other citizens and they cannot make ends meet.
This is why there are so many problems in agriculture as in other areas of the economy. People cannot operate their farm on a profitable basis any more, excepted larger organizations. Those can finally survive but the ordinary owner of a family operation cannot make ends meet.
So, if we want agriculture to be more prosperous, we will have to find mechanisms other than the traditional ones. We cannot seem to find any logical formula to really stimulate agriculture. Yet the incentive formula is always the same: we have to try to find ways to lower prices through the granting of compensated discounts, the lowering of interest rates, through allowing the purchase of cheap machinery and eliminating taxes on building materials and on all kinds of goods.
That is a way, Mr. Chairman, to stimulate agriculture for the greater prosperity of Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a short intervention on this item. When the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar was speaking, he said he was dealing
Supply
specifically with two areas. I also wish to touch on those two areas. I regret that the hon. member is not here at the moment. In the latter stages of his remarks the hon. member said that he wondered what our position was with regard to the marketing of rapeseed and whether rapeseed should be handled by the Canadian Wheat Board. He said something about my having made some vague utterance on this question.
We have been anything but vague. We have taken the position that it is up to the producers to decide this issue. In our discussions with producers we have followed their advice that a significant amount of information is needed about the marketing system, the open market, a pooled market, Wheat Board marketing, and that this must be in the producers' hands before they can make a sensible decision about which kind of marketing they want. It is our position that it is up to the producers to decide.
I know that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar comes from a party which on the provincial side in Saskatchewan seems to take the view that it ought to decide when producers should have a marketing board, whether the producers want one or not, and goes ahead with marketing boards without consulting producers and imposes upon them a particular solution. That is in keeping with the basic NDP philosophy that the experts, that is to say themselves, ought to tell producers and everyone else what to do, and they will be better off for having been told.
I think that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar is quite right in wondering about the Conservative position on this issue. He stated he would like to give them five minutes in which to present their views. I think it would be more workable if he were to invite five or six of them to state their five or six views on this issue, since usually their position on agricultural questions varies from one part of the country to another; they have no consensus. Luckily, they have not so far needed to reach a consensus on any of these issues.
If the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar has missed our position, or found it vague, let me state it for him once again very clearly. We will not impose producer marketing boards upon the producers of rapeseed, but we are prepared to offer them this type of marketing should they choose it. We have waited until they themselves are able to say that the information has been in their hands long enough to enable appropriate consultations to be held. I should like to repeat what I have said to some producer organizations and their representatives in the last few weeks: I believe the time is now ripe for us to take that next step and consult producers about the kind of marketing they want.
The member for Saskatoon-Biggar referred to price differentials which can exist under the present system. He referred to farmers who sell at a lower price at one period of the year and who then find that their neighbours are selling at a different price in another period of the year. This, of course, is one of the annoyances which will lead some producers to opt for board marketing, which will lead some producers to choose to get out of the business of speculating directly on the rapeseed market; they wish

Supply
to farm to raise the grain, not to speculate in its sale. This leads them to prefer the board marketing system.
Other producers, of course, have taken the view that the rapeseed market has been doing very well, that the price has been high and that the product has been moving. This is the aspect they are apt to stress in their arguments with other producers on this question. Let hon. members have no doubt about this, however: we propose to proceed by holding consultations on this question with producers in the very near future as to the kind of marketing system they prefer and then to move in accordance with their wishes, given the support of the House of Commons for the principle-a sensible one in my view-that machinery should be available to enable producers to handle their products in the way that producers desire.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar-I am glad to see him back in his place-also dealt with the need to provide relief for farmers whose crops suffer from particularly adverse weather conditions. He said there was a need for the Minister of Agriculture to view the scene in person. The Minister of Agriculture is an extremely energetic and sympathetic man who is going about his duties with tremendous enthusiasm and with the interest of the farmers very much at heart. He is away, necessarily, for several hours this afternoon on official business. On his behalf as well as on my own I should like to say a few words on this subject.
Hon. members are apt to ignore the fact that the provinces have some very important responsibilities in the field of agriculture. The hon. member says the Minister of Agriculture should personally visit the scene of these crop failures. Mr. Speaker, when localized problems occur it is particular fitting that provincial ministers of agriculture should take a lead and deal with them. This has been the position of the federal government for some time with respect to problems which can arise in localized areas, whether they involve fire or flood or unusual weather conditions.
Essentially, responsibility lies within the area in which the setback occurs. The federal government is ready to assist when the magnitude of the problem is so great that the burden would be too much for the provincial government concerned to bear. Notwithstanding this general rule, we have involved ourselves to the extent of strengthening the hand of the provincial ministers of agriculture both in eastern and in western Canada by offering certain forms of assistance in situations of this kind.
There are certain difficulties attached to rushing in with assistance when particular problems involving crop damage occur. Crop insurance programs across this country have been developed as a result of initiatives taken by this government and its predecessor. The usefulness of the program is gradually improving, and consequent upon the step now proposed, in accordance with which the federal government would bear an even greater share of the cost of the premiums across the country, it may improve even further. It is, of course, important that the crop insurance plans should be good plans and that farmers take advantage of what is, after all, the main measure of insurance against the occasional disaster which might occur. To some extent the provision of special assistance

militates against the development of good crop insurance plans.
I should also like to draw attention two ways in which other governments have acted to assist areas in which weather conditions, particularly in early winter, give rise to chronic problems. There is the forage incentive program, now going into its third year of operation, under which some 3.7 million acres have already been taken from grain production and put to grass and forage as a base for livestock industries and to enable farmers to raise produce which is free from certain hazards such as early snow which can afflict wheat, barley and other grain crops.
I am happy to note that applications for payment under the forage incentive program came largely from areas in which the cattle industry should develop, areas in which grain production may be hazardous because of the recurrence of unfavourable weather conditions year after year. It is also the case that over the past three years we have offset some of the problems which arose in connection with the production of barley in those areas, thus making it easier for farmers to switch some of the risk away from themselves by planting barley instead of wheat. We achieved this result by revising the quota system in a way which brought about equality of treatment for barley growers as compared with wheat growers. We did it by carefully watching the initial prices for barley to ensure that they were attractive. In doing this we benefited the whole country by assuring new feed grain markets, markets which had for so long been neglected in this country. We have now gone into them in a big way. Barley is being grown in those areas where the climate is conducive to the shorter maturing period required by that crop, to the benefit of the farmers directly concerned and also to the national good.
This year we have also taken advantage of legislation passed by parliament at the initiative of the Liberal government two and a half years ago. I refer to the ability to extend by order in council cash advances in relation to grain which is still unharvested. This is a modest form of assistance but a useful one, so useful that in two previous periods it received special attention in the House in the form of legislation to enable the government to extend those provisions to the farmers affected. We have been able to do this by order in council as a result of the foresight shown on the last occasion when this question was discussed. On that occasion the provision to which I have referred was specifically embodied in the law.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar inquired about present Wheat Board cash advances. I have already discussed this subject with officials of the Wheat Board as a result of my own concern about the position of farmers who find themselves in a difficult financial situation as a result of adverse weather conditions-farmers who are in arrears in their repayments and in whose case the Wheat Board feels it is necessary to take some action to protect its own position. I am afraid that the position in which the Wheat Board finds itself is such as to require some steps to be taken in connection with these arrears. The farmers in question had undertaken to be in possession of adequate grain to repay the advances at the time they took out the initial advance. This has created some difficulties.
February 12, 1973

I have discussed the seed grain situation with the Minister of Agriculture. He will certainly see to it that should there be a shortage steps will be taken to ensure that supplies are available.
The government has been attempting not only to assist farmers in difficult financial situations but to encourage the production of crops which are most suited to particular areas as a means of minimizing the size of losses which can occur. I am happy that notwithstanding certain criticisms, the gist of the hon. member's remarks has been to support the measures which have been taken.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hardly thought when I returned to the House of Commons that my first speech would be on agriculture, but this seems to be my fate. I rise to say a few words to the absent Minister of Agriculture, not only to give him condolences for his job but to support him in what I suspect is his new, fresh attitude toward the marketing of grain in this country. When three weeks ago he asked the farmers of western Canada to grow all the grain they could, I was in western Canada and supported those remarks because they were the direct opposite of what we had been told for the previous four years.
Votes before the committee of $8 million or $9 million, money to help farmers in great distress, can only be understood by the rest of the country when we look at the whole situation in perspective. The perspective of the last four years has been of a government that is going the wrong way in the matter of marketing, that has been reducing the income of farmers to a level where they could not build up reserves with which to meet the emergencies that occur, whether they be in the Peace River area, eastern Ontario, the Maritimes or the eastern townships of Quebec. That was a deliberate decision made by the government of the day after three years of study, and it sent this country in the wrong direction.
Today this country stands condemned in the eyes of the hungry people of this world for not being able to do what it is elementary that we do here, namely, produce food for the world, something we can do so efficiently. By letting the income of our farmers decline to the point it reached in 1969 and 1970 we took away the farmers' ability to produce food and meet the demands of the world.
It is a matter of shame to every Canadian who ponders about this interdependent world in which we live that for the last four years Canada has been a net importer of beef at a time when the world is desperately short of protein. No government sitting in the seat of power during the last four years can escape that indictment. It is no help to the people around the world who need that protein to say that our American neighbours are also importing beef, because their government stands condemned for the same reason. The United States took land out of production and applied restrictions. That is why today the American farmers, indeed the American people, stand beside Canadians equal in guilt and equal in shame for not doing the basic things they should have done.
It is on the subject of grain that I want to speak most strongly. I shall praise the Minister of Agriculture so long as he keeps going in the direction he is going now, namely,
Supply
that of expanding production. When there is a hungry world, any minister or any government that votes for restricting the production of food in a country that can produce food as Canada can stands condemned not only before parliament but before the country and their own conscience. I want to make that very clear.
There has been a debate all over the western world this last 15 to 20 years about the future of agriculture. World economists have been looking at the traditional markets for certain products. To use wheat as an example, in our traditional bread-grain markets of Europe these economists see a declining per capita consumption of bread-grains, and since the population is not increasing quickly enough to take up the slack these economists say that we must advise our farmers in the bread growing areas of the world to reduce production.
They do not see in that model two billion people living in Asia, South America and Africa who would like access to any type of food whether traditional with them or not. They do not see in that model that China has now come into the market as a steady purchaser of bread-grains from western countries. They do not see in that model that they use that Russia, having spread its agricultural production across the Urals and into the volatile, dry land of that area, sporadically comes into the market to buy several hundred million bushels of grain. They do not see any of these new factors in that model. They do not see in the general picture that whereas ten years ago the average trade in wheat between the countries of the world was roughly one billion bushels a year, it is today over two billion bushels a year and is still rising. What was a surplus ten years ago is nothing at all today.
When so much was said in this House two years ago about surplus there was roughly a surplus of two and a half billion bushels of grain, insufficient for one year's marketing. No merchant can stay in business without having something on the shelves, but we took our inventory off the shelves. That is what I want to speak about, Mr. Chairman, putting it in very simple terms.
In addition to the advice given to us by economists, advice was also given to us by those who know the needs of people-nutritionists, demographers, sociologists. A conference was held here in Canada in June of 1969, the first and only conference of this kind held in Canada, attended by all the brains of the Ford Foundation, the Rockefeller Foundation and the Food and Agriculture Organization, etc. At this conference representatives told of all they had done to bring about a green revolution around the world and confessed that even with all their efforts in the waters of the sea and on the dry land areas of the world, they would be unable to meet the needs of the people of the world. Therefore, they pleaded with governments to go all out to produce all the food they could. Figures were cited showing how they were losing the race.
The minister of agriculture in the previous government, the Hon. H. A. Olson, was given this information and he attended the November meeting in Rome of FAO. On November 11 he stood before the FAO nations and pledged Canada's all-out support for the expansion of production to help meet the deficiency in food production around the world. He made that pledge on our behalf.

February 12, 1973
Supply
Three months later it was repudiated in this House and in the country.
Mr. Chairman, I have got to the point in my remarks where I should like to make them cohesive, so may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was in the process of putting before it the type of decision the government made some three years ago which was so disastrous to the farmers of western Canada and to the world as a whole. I described one type of advice coming from the nutritionists, to the effect that no matter what we could do, we could not begin to feed the world and meet the gap which existed between the needs and our ability to supply. On the other hand, there was advice coming from economists mainly, to the effect that governments in the western world should restrict production and match production to the markets in our traditional areas.
To show that this debate was a lively one I hold up to the committee, as an example, the speech delivered by the then minister of agriculture, the Hon. H. A. Olson, in which he quoted figures from nutritionists pointing out that we produced only a certain amount of food in the world but that needs were roughly one-third higher. This speech was delivered on November 11, 1969, by the then Canadian minister of agriculture to the FAO. Three months later, on February 27, 1970, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board made a statement in the House of Commons to the effect that we had too much wheat on hand, requiring farmers, by inducement and by force, to stop producing wheat in the year 1970. That policy enunciated by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board was a strike in the back of his colleague the minister of agriculture which destroyed that minister before the producers of western Canada.
When the then minister of agriculture took that stand in November, 1969, I am positive he did so with all the honesty of any minister of agriculture speaking on a subject so important to his portfolio. In the meantime, the government-and I can only assume it was the minister in charge of the Wheat Board who had the biggest say- reversed the policy and the direction of the minister of agriculture by coming out for restriction with the Lift program which is supposed to mean "lower inventory for tomorrow" but which turned out to be "lower income for tomorrow." That is why the farmers in Peace River and in

every other part of the country who have been smashed about by this government for the last four or five years cannot cope with this emergency situation with which we are now faced.
That decision by the government in February, 1970, was only part of a four-point program or package to restrict agriculture. The first as the Lift program to stop wheat production in western Canada for that year. Secondly, the government brought in a marketing act, the infamous Bill C-176, as a result of which farmers were not given control over their agriculture; control and decision-making in every step of agriculture from seeding to selling was put under the power of civil servants, with no control by parliament and no control by the farmers. It was a terrific example of controls and restriction on agriculture along the lines that economists of Europe, and later of North America, advocated. Thirdly, we had the stabilization bill. This bill meant that if you did what civil servants told you to do, you would be eligible for a formula-type minimum wage on the farm of $2,000 a year. I will not go into detail as to what happened to these bills.
The fourth part of the package was the adjustment program. This was a program aimed, as the task force had recommended in 1969, at getting two out of every three farmers in every part of Canada-not just in the west-off the farm, and the farmers in the west to cut grain acreage in half. This four-point program was the result of an economic theory called supply-management. This supply-management theory was in control and was running the government; the ministers had no say and I do not think the government understood what they were walking into. The time when appointed officials of government can run the elected officials of government is about over, and that is what the issue was across this country last year.
I have spoken of these two speeches and have indicated to the committee what the issues were. I simply point out that as a result of these restrictive policies and the whole direction the government took-and it was a wrong direction-income which from 1953 to 1957 had been about $2,000 a year for farmers in Saskatchewan and had slowly climbed from 1961 to 1967 to about $6,000 a year suddenly went down to $2,000 a year. Yet the experts ask me why the west went against the government. If your income had been $2,000, and it went up to $6,000 and then back down to $2,000, would you not think that the government was a wrong-way government? Only one Liberal outside the city of Winnipeg survived the feelings of westerners.
I think I have said enough to illustrate the fact that we have had a wrong-way government because we have had wrong-way ministers. We have had a fire-sale government which in spite of shortages a year and a half ago forced the sale of grain regardless of price, and they come along now and tell us to look at all the bushels they have sold. I know it is hard to explain to non-farmers how the impact of this situation hits the western farmer. If you ran a car lot which was facing another car lot on the other side of the street, and you left an agent in charge while you were away and came back after a short trip to find all your cars were sold, you might say, "What a good boy he is." But if you found he sold all the cars at below cost, you were
February 12, 1973

broke and the guy across the street was still in business, I am sure you would get rid of that salesman.
This fire-sale attitude is the basic reason for the troubles the government is now facing. This is the basic reason for many people around this world suffering a food shortage. They are short of rice in Southeast Asia, and short of wheat all over the world; yet we sit with relatively nothing to sell because of this policy forcing the farmers to sell, not on an orderly basis according to the Wheat Board but through fire-sale type activity.
We tried to get rid of this situation 35 or 37 years ago when we set up the Canadian Wheat Board. However, this government has hit farmers so hard during the last four years that it will take a generation to remove the monument in their minds which says that the Lift program is a program to take farmers out of production. Now, when the price is up to $3 per bushel, there is no grain to sell. The government has just begun to pay the price of that folly.
My final words to the absent Minister of Agriculture are to keep his back close to the wall and not to let them do to him what they did to Olson. In the last days of the campaign Olson said that the Lift program was the greatest mistake of his life. It was not only the greatest mistake of his life; it was the greatest mistake of every member of the government and everybody else who supported that program, because they betrayed not only the farmers but also the hungry peoples of the world. That is the indictment of this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise with pleasure following the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who is back with us in this House after a period of absence. I do so with pleasure because after the recent election campaign the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain had been saying things far apart from what his leader and other agricultural critics of his party had been saying and they found it necessary to make him the critic for energy, mines and resources.
You may not know this, Mr. Chairman, but during the course of the election campaign the Conservative platform contained a promise that the initial price for wheat should go up by 30 cents a bushel. At that time it was $1.45 a bushel. Shortly thereafter the world price began moving very rapidly, and in order to put funds into the hands of the farmers we raised the price of wheat by 31 cents a bushel compared to the 30 cents a bushel the opposition was advocating. Then they did not know whether they were promising an additional 30 cents a bushel or what. This is part of their policy which allowed them to speak in different tongues in different parts of the country.
I know my own opponent wanted to get one step up, so he said that their 30 cents would be in addition to what the Liberals had done. That set me back a little until the Leader of the Opposition was in town the next day and said that now the Liberals had done exactly what the Conservatives had promised. I should say to hon. members that the initial price at $1.76 meant an elevator price of perhaps in the order of $1.47 or $1.50 depending on
Supply
where you are, which the Leader of the Opposition said they had promised while my opponent said they would go 30 cents better. That, of course, did not bother the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain because he had promised a $2 price at the elevator right from the beginning and he was able to stand with that. However, as I say they made him responsible for the field of energy, mines and resources rather than grain. We have to admit that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain is the visionary of his party. Of course, everybody knows what a visionary is; in the Tory party a visionary is someone who after something has happened can in fact see it clearly.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
I say that particularly in relation to what the hon. member has just said in speaking about the Lift program. He should go back over the remarks of his colleagues in the House at the time the Lift program was announced. Their criticism ranged from the fact that it would not do any good because, with all that summer fallow, the next year as much grain would be grown again and we would be back with the same problem we had in the first place. That is the kind of line they were taking.
The point, of course, is that they talked about our having to sell a lot more grain than we were. They tried to talk about the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain as their great salesman. It turns out that for the past several years the best year for sales while he was Minister of Agriculture responsible for the Wheat Board has been far surpassed. In fact, I expect within a matter of months to be able to report to the House that we have sold as much in a year as he sold in the best two years put together.
The years in which the hon. member was responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board were years of building elevators in the prairie region. He built more elevators and just put more grain into them. He never really sold as much as was being produced. The farmers were complaining more and more about the problem of accumulated grain. Then along came my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs who had some golden years during which grain moved very rapidly out of the country in record volumes-close to 700 million bushels. Indeed, when he was minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board he had to ask the Wheat Board questions which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain never had to ask, namely, how much was it possible to carry out of the country with the existing handling and transportation system, a system which of course had been inherited in the previous five years from the Conservative government of which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was the key minister in this field. My colleague was told what the limits were and he exported grain in those years when he was responsible at a record level, with the handling and transportation system which we had-a level which was not even conceived of when the hon. member opposite was the minister responsible. That is the fact of the matter with regard to where our grain situation stood.
The hon. member has just made an impassioned speech about how we should be feeding the poor peoples of the world and should have gone on growing grain for them.

February 12, 1973
Supply
Let me ask hon. members whether through 1968-69 and 1969-70, when we had large surpluses of grain in this country, they were treated as assets by our buyers around the world. Not a bit of it. They were treated as reasons for depressing the price. It was not until the United States finally made a large sale of grain to Russia this year-and it probably did not involve as much as we adjusted our inventory by during 1970-that there was a dramatic impact upon the world price and we started to get for our farmers a fair price for grain, a price not below the cost of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
The facts of the matter are that we had an inventory in this country which was treated by all our farmers as being a significant problem. Indeed, if the hon. member will look back at the speeches of his colleague he will find that they were complaining about the Lift program partly because they said tnose farmers who saw the surplus problem as a real problem had already done something about it, and that now we were bringing in a program which did not allow for the fact that they had already coped with the problem. That was the kind of criticism they levelled at us. They saw that that kind of supply on hand was in fact a problem; it was a price depressant problem in the world.
We were told that we should go out and sell grain. I said at that time, and we did it, that we would sell grain at record volumes year after year notwithstanding this program. In the very best year while the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain had responsibility for the Wheat Board we had an export figure of 453 million bushels. When I first asked the Canadian Wheat Board whether it could in fact handle an export of 800 million bushels, I was told it could perhaps handle 700 million bushels. In the year 1970-71 we went beyond 700 million bushels; we reached a figure of 706 million bushels. Last year we exported 824 million bushels. This year, with grain at record prices, we are exporting at new record volumes and can go on into next year exporting again at record volumes, notwithstanding what the hon. member says about supply.
Of course, we know the hon. member said we should have realized the desirability of moving into beef production. He was not here and perhaps has forgotten that with the Lift program we went into a forage incentive program to encourage the cattle industry. When that was over we offered the prairie farmers $40 million at $10 an acre to move grain land into grass because we believed there was a future in beef and that was what we should be producing. We talked about diversification into meat and into barley. I wonder whether the hon. member knows what the word barley means.

never promoted to any significant degree in foreign markets. Members from the Tory party are rankling at that and they ask: what are the facts?

We turned our attention to barley in a big way. We said that we should get into the feed grain markets of the world and we asked the Wheat Board to go to work to market that grain. And they did. When I spoke earlier I referred to the Minister of Justice in his capacity as minister responsible for the Wheat Board striking down his colleague, the ex-minister of agriculture, Mr. Olson, who had come out on Canada's behalf with pledges for an all-out production of grain. The minister came along three months later and said "There is too much grain. Cut down all wheat acreage in 1970." That is the monument that the farmers will carry of him as long as they live.
Now, as for that little highschool boy chit-chat about the initial price, it was clear to us a year and a half ago that Russia was in trouble with the winter wheat crop. The right hon. member for Prince Albert spoke up in this House on several occasions and asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board when was he going to raise the price to take advantage of this great demand for grain. All the minister could come back and say was, "The Americans won't raise the price." Mr. Chairman, when was there a law in this country which said Canadians could not raise the price? Never in the history of parliament has any minister ever stood up and said he had no right to have any say about the future and the prices of our products, that he had to run down to the U.S.A. and ask the people who have led this whole supply-management nonsense for the last 15 years, "Won't you raise the price?"
Do you think the farmers are going to be happy with all these statistics and figures when they sit on their farms with almost empty granaries and when they know that the grain they grew over the last five or six years was dumped on the market in 1971 and 1972 at a price below the cost of production? Now they sit there with empty granaries when grain is selling at $3 a bushel and the minister sits here in this House and says, "What a good boy am I." Mr. Chairman, he is the boy who took over the automobile lot and sold all the cars at half price before the boss came back. The boss in this case is the voter, and he will clean out the Liberals.
With respect to the initial price, our party met in Saskatoon in June last year. We asked the party to accept the fact that prices had to go up and that the farmers should be told and given a little hope. We said we should increase the initial price of all three main grains. As a matter of fact, we announced that officially at the beginning of the election campaign. Then the minister became terrified that he might lose a vote in Saskatoon-Humboldt and he raised the initial prices by the same amount that we advocated. This does not mean one cent more to the farmer, Mr. Chairman; he simply gets some money into his hands earlier.
Now I want to come to the main issue and get to real grips with the minister. During the campaign, Mr. Chairman, not only did I support the raising of the initial price

but I called for a price of $2 at Thunder Bay and I said there would be no trouble about reaching it because the price would go to $2.50 by Christmas. I was wrong; it went up to nearly $3. But you have to give farmers some hope when they are broke, particularly after four years of government under the leadership of the type given by the Minister of Justice. Long betore the price rose above $1.75, where this minister was keeping it, I said it should be $2.1 won't go back over all that hash. But back in 1953 to 1957 in western Canada we piled up wheat. Then the government changed and in 1961 and 1962 we gave open quotas to the farmers and all the grain they could produce was sold.

It was not
pleasant for me, Mr. Chairman, to sit out of parliament later and watch the succeeding government, with its restrictive measures, bring that average income down from $6,000 to $2,000 in the years 1969 and 1970. I don't care how many bushels you sell, it is what is left in your pocket when you have sold it that counts. It is for this that we hold the government guilty.
Now we sit here with a hungry world around us, with race riots all through Southeast Asia because of hunger, with trouble in Pakistan, India and Afghanistan and we cannot help those peoples because we do not have the grain. Russia still wants grain. The wheat farmer in Russia is in trouble again this year. Russia wants more grain this year. Where are we going to get it? 1 am glad that this debate is taking place. What is the point of the minister saying, "Look at all the bushels I have sold," when the farmers are broke? Why are we voting this money to help the farmers in the Peace River area? It is because they do not have money to cope with a local, one year disaster. It would be the same in any part of the grain area.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the minister mentioned barley. That is a word he should not have mentioned. We all know about his barley goings on. Barley is a coarse grain that used to be produced for making beer. Then the Americans found a way to produce their own barley to make their own beer, and that market went to pieces. But ever since 1960-61 there has been a rising demand for coarse grains around the world, including barley, not for making beer but for feeding animals. The minister is quite correct when he says that the best future for grain is going to be in the feed grains, not just the bread-grains. I am not

arguing that at all; what I am arguing about is this barley business.
Somebody gave orders to the Canadian Wheat Board in April, 1970, when the farmers were rising in protest against Operation Lift all over the three prairie provinces, and told the Wheat Board to break the law, not to follow the processes of orderly marketing but to dump barley onto the world markets. In the succeeding months the Wheat Board dumped millions and millions of bushels of western barley on world markets; in fact, there was not enough to meet all the feed contracts so in 1971 the minister went out and said to the farmers, "Grow all the barley you can." The farmers looked in the newspapers and saw that the price was $1.30 at Thunder Bay. They said that that was pretty good and so they grew 161 million bushels of barley in 1971. But in 1972, when they went to get the extra above the initial payment, what did they get? They got zero, Mr. Chairman, and there was a loss on the pool of $11 million. This is what we want the minister to explain in committee, not here. There are more angry barley farmers around Saskatchewan than you will find in any other part of the world, and the minister should know that.
Now to deal with diversification. That action was taken by somebody frightened by the fuss farmers were raising about the Lift program. That somebody said, "We have to get money into the farmers' hands. Sell something." The only competition they had to sell against was an American broker down in Duluth who had 20 million bushels of rotten barley in his granaries which he was trying to get rid of for 57 cents or 58 cents a bushel. We sold our barley in competition with rotten barley in a bin in Duluth. Who was this person who interfered and intervened with the Wheat Board? I want to know, and so do a lot of farmers. We want to find out who gave that order. It was not orderly marketing; it was fire-sale marketing. The law says that the Wheat Board is to sell grain at the best possible price for the advantage of the western farmer. But somebody interfered, somebody monkeyed. And somebody has to pay the price. These are the reasons we on this side of the House want some answers from the government.
It is all very fine to vote a $400 grant each to a group of farmers who have been hard hit this year. But that does not cover the gap between conscience and fact. The fact is that the farmers have been betrayed. The farmers have not had their grain sold at above cost. The farmers have not seen the government renew these long-term agreements with the iron curtain countries. The farmers have seen everything that they had hoped and dreamed of in the years 1965 to 1967, when everything was looking up for them, destroyed under the present Minister of Justice who thinks that because he is from Saskatchewan he is the natural crown prince of the Liberal party.

We have a lot of patience, Mr. Chairman. I should like to point out the necessity of encouraging prairie farmers to produce enough barley and rapeseed to meet market demands at a time when world wheat demand is at record levels. To reduce the supply of other grains may limit the future markets for these alternate crops.
I know that people in the prairie provinces are very concerned that production of some of the other crops will be neglected and they do not want to see this happen. We ought to encourage production of specialty crops such as rapeseed, rye, flax and barley-particularly rapeseed. The federal government should establish an incentives policy for producers of field grains to encourage sufficient acreage to ensure adequate supplies. One step to encourage production of grains other than wheat would be to increase the guaranteed initial payment for barley by at least 15 cents a bushel before seeding in the spring of 1973.
In Saskatchewan we would like to use most of the feed grains we produce to feed our own hogs and cattle, and we would like to develop our own meat packing industry and the secondary industries as well. When we produce enough for export we will gladly ship it to Ontario and Quebec as well as to the overseas markets. If the federal government desires or demands changes in production patterns or a variety of changes for some reason or other, financial incentives should be provided to producers to make the required adjustment.
I should like to say a word or two about the international trade in grains, Mr. Chairman. Since the price range in the International Grains Agreement collapsed in 1971 the world has not had effective international agreements for trade in grains. The present International Wheat Agreement which began in mid-1971 runs to mid-1974 but it does not have any price ranges at all. Producers and consumers of grain, especially wheat, are best served by an effective and strong international agreement concerning price, supply and trading conditions.
I urge the minister responsible for the Wheat Board to work with vigour to develop a climate in which a new and effective agreement may be forged after the present one expires. Things are looking better on the Prairies, Mr. Chairman, and we do not want the things that happened four or five or ten or 15 years ago to happen again. In the west we want to look to the future and make our agricultural economy more stable. The new agreement which, hopefully, will be negotiated by 1974 will cover wheat and also feed grains.
This international agreement on grains should also include national and foreign stockholding policies, maintenance of adequate reserves, a reduction of trade barriers through commitment by exporters and importers, co-ordination of farm programs, maximum and minimum prices for world transactions and adequate food aid.

Now that the war in Viet Nam is over and people are still dying of starvation in Bangladesh, perhaps we should be laying aside a few million bushels to aid these war ravaged countries.
With regard to marketing, Mr. Chairman, I feel that the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board should be extended to cover the marketing of rapeseed, rye and flax. A recent study committee established by the federal grains group recommended that producers be provided an opportunity to say by plebiscite whether they support the present rapeseed marketing system or an alternative. I support the proposal for a plebiscite, as does my riding, and I urge producers to support the alternative which would give marketing authority over rapeseed to the Canadian Wheat Board.
Rapeseed is produced in my constituency and some is shipped to Vancouver and some to Thunder Bay. Because the futures market in Vancouver is consistently higher than in Thunder Bay, the result is that some points in Saskatchewan have a great differential in rapeseed prices although they are very close together geographically. On October 6, 1972, the price of rapeseed in Glaslyn was 23 cents a bushel more than at Meadow Lake. I was home to Shellbrook last weekend. I talked to many farmers at a hockey match. They told me that in the village of Leask the price of grain was 31 cents more than at Shellbrook. These two villages are 25 miles apart. What is disconcerting is that rapeseed packed into boxcars in Saskatchewan is shipped from Leask through Shellbrook to Prince Albert and on to the west coast, yet the producer of Shellbrook received 31 cents less last week.

We should try to solve this problem, Mr. Chairman. Certainly this anomaly would be liquidated if prices were administered by the Wheat Board and the price of rapeseed was averaged. The only people benefiting now are the boys playing the futures market. There is a lobby in this House of people who are not interested in the welfare of the farmer but in the futures market or grain exchange operations at Winnipeg, or Vancouver, if there is one there.
Consequently, I suggest-and I believe this is part of the policy of the Saskatchewan wheat pool-(a) that the federal government introduce necessary legislation immediately which would give authority to the Canadian Wheat Board to market rapeseed; (b) that a producers' plebiscite be held to determine whether producers support extension of Wheat Board powers to the marketing of rapeseed; and (c) that any permit holder who has produced rapeseed in any one or more of the last three crop years be eligible to vote on this question and that a simple majority of those voting be required in favour before the marketing authority be given to the board. I think this is one step that can be taken immediately. It would be progressive.
Before produce can be marketed, it has to be moved. We hear a lot about occasional grain tie-ups on the west coast or at Thunder Bay. Personally, I favour nationalization of the grain handling system at Vancouver so that it is divorced from other work stoppages at that port. No
[Mr. Nesdoly.J
farmer should be expected to haul his grain more than 25 miles under most circumstances. If the suggested rail lines are abandoned, some farmers will have to haul their grain 50 miles to market. I suggest that the scheduled abandonment of railroad lines be postponed until this entire matter is thoroughly studied to determine its effect on marketing and the movement of grain.
We are debating payments to farmers under farm income maintenance. Because of poor whether conditions and other risks associated with agriculture, we in this House should not begrudge the payment of moneys to farmers who have suffered crop losses. I am certainly in support of them. Perhaps they are not enough.
I hope this House will take some long-term measures in the direction of comprehensive crop insurance programs to ensure that every producer of crops in this country has some kind of insurance so that eventually there will be no need to debate in this House year after year crop losses in one part of Canada or another. This would necessitate co-operation between the federal and provincial governments.
As far as the estimates of production and marketing and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board are concerned, I am in agreement with them and I hope we can soon bring this matter to a vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the production, marketing and transportation of our grains. Lately, a lot of fellows have been talking who have not produced too many bushels of wheat or barley. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board, and my friend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, covered a lot of ground in a very few minutes.
There are a few things I would like to say about this world of wheat in which we live. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is on pretty shaky ground when he starts patting himself on the back for the record exports that Canada is now enjoying, because last year 60 per cent of Canadian wheat exports went to production catastrophe areas around the world. That is a pretty shaky basis on which to build some stability into our grain industry. If anyone knows anything about grain, they know that Canada does not sell grain to Russia, India or Pakistan; those people come here and purchase it.
For five consecutive years western farmers saw farm deliveries of wheat go down, down, down. We ended up with a four-bushel quota with production controls in the torm of Operation Lift around our neck. Farmers were ready to rebel. That is when the word came out for the Wheat Board to sell barley. I was on the floor of the Winnipeg exchange the day the Wheat Board offered its barley to the world. The big international traders could not believe what they were hearing. They got their hands on 150 million bushels of barley at a fire-sale price. That deal cost the western farmers $50 million.
The other day we were discussing the purchase of hopper cars. It was ironic that at the very time these estimates were being discussed in committee, American grain for export was being moved through Canada in Canadian cars over Canadian rails to Seattle. I received several calls that day from farmers in Saskatchewan com-
February 12, 1973

meriting on the large number of Canadian cars in Montana and Dakota sitting on sidings. In one case, 52 empty Canadian boxcars had been there for over seven days. I want to read a statement given by a grain farmer to the press in southern Saskatchewan:
Since the first of December, four or five hundred Canadian boxcars full of American grain have entered Canada at North Portal, Saskatchewan, gone up the Soo line, on to B.C., and then down into the states for export out of Seattle.
The farmer said he is critical of Canadian Pacific Railway for allowing the Americans to use Canadian cars and Canadian rail lines to move grain to coastal terminals when there is difficulty in having Canadian grain moved to the west coast. He said:
As an example, North Portal has a six-bushel quota on wheat, and has trouble getting enough cars. But U.S. wheat moves right through there in Canadian boxcars.
The farmer then asked what sense there was in providing the railways with 2,000 additional cars so that it could take its own cars out of service and rent them to the Americans. The CPR claim they are up to date on all Wheat Board deliveries to Thunder Bay and the west coast. The point I am making is that there is no shortage of grain cars in Canada over-all, even now when we are in the midst of a record grain movement.
Senior officials of both railroads have given assurances in the past that they could move one billion bushels to export with the equipment they already have, given a degree of co-operation and planning. Our number one grain transportation problem has not been the number of grain cars available; it has been to get the cars through the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific seaboard so that the grain will be available to our customers when they want it and so that Canada could be classed as a dependable supplier. We must have some order of priorities, some long-range plans so that all segments of the grain industry, railroads, shippers, handling companies and, most important of all, producers will be able to see the future with some intelligence.
We on the Prairies are stunned by talk of spending hundreds of millions of dollars on new airports and hundreds of millions more on pipelines into the frozen north when we cannot now depend on getting our produce to the customers to their satisfaction. I was on board a Japanese ship in Vancouver just about a year ago. That vessel had been waiting there for 37 days to take on a cargo of Canadian feed barley. They hadn't taken on a single bushel. According to the captain, the cost of maintaining a vessel there was some $4,000 a day. Thirty-seven days at $4,000 a day-all of which will be paid for in demurrage and higher ocean freight by the western farmers!
Year after year thousands of loaded grain cars are trapped east of the Rocky Mountains because of the Fraser canyon. Last year the Canadian National line to Prince Rupert was blocked for five weeks. The Canadian Pacific track was blocked for four weeks through the Fraser canyon. Winter comes each year; and labour problems will continue to plague us. This $48 million expenditure will not solve our number one grain transportation problem, which is getting our product to the Pacific sea-
Supply
board. More than 40 per cent of Canada's grain exports go out by way of the Pacific seaboard, yet the seaboard possesses only 10 per cent of Canada's terminal elevator capacity.
It is obvious that the present system has no capacity to stockpile. As a matter of fact, five million to seven million bushels of wheat is about the best they can do at the west coast-about a three-day supply at full loading rate. We are in good shape this year. Nature has been kind to us. The railroads have not been blocked. Vessels are arriving on time. There is no tough or damp grain. And there are no labour problems. According to the Canadian Grains Commission report for the week ending January 24, there were 6,853,000 bushels of milling wheat in seven terminals at the Pacific seaboard. Over a million bushels of that were in Prince Rupert. On the average, this is less than a boatload at each of the Vancouver and Victoria terminals.
Competing with western grain farmers for transportation to the west coast are coal, potash and sulphur. These commodities are handled in solid train and unit train lots through modern bulk handling facilities. There is a capacity for stockpiling for weeks ahead, thereby protecting customers against the consequences of railway stoppages. As the total tonnage handled by the railways continues to build rapidly, the grain export situation becomes more critical with each passing year. Grain, the only commodity under government control, is the one that suffers most.
The government of Canada conducted a three-year study of grain transportation at great cost to the taxpayers. Instead of acting on the report, hon. gentlemen opposite turned this hot potato over to the Canada Grains Council which now estimates it would take another five years to finalize. The expenditure of $48 million on these hopper cars was made for reasons of political expediency. It was announced by the Prime Minister in Winnipeg where it would make the biggest political impact just before the last election.
What we should be doing is using to the maximum the facilities which are already in existence. It is almost incredible that during the three-year transportation study nobody in the federal government ever contacted the bulk handling people in Vancouver-people whose systems contain unused capacity and who are ready, willing and able to help export more grain. The expenditure at the Pacific seaboard of a small portion of the $48 million spent on new grain cars would have increased the throughput of grain at Vancouver by more than a third, more than 100 million bushels a year. It would have allowed us to stockpile against rail stoppages and enabled us to use modern bulk loading facilities to compete with the coal, potash and sulphur moving to export.
A good deal has been said about the Lift program. I shall not say anything more about that. I will say that in 1971 the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board went on record advocating the need for additional grain storage at the west coast. Our good customers, the Japanese, took the unprecedented step of sponsoring a transportation conference in Vancouver as a means of expressing their growing concern. However, the desire of the producers to move more grain to export and the custom-

ers' pleas for better west coast service have both gone unheeded.
We could and we should be selling and exporting more grain. On September 13, 1972, the Kansas City board of trade, talking about the tremendous increase in wheat prices, released the following news item from which I quote:
-but in Canada's case the increases were almost academic because that country was not booking any shipments at the higher prices, due to the fact that it had already sold all it could move overseas until May of next year.
With wheat quoted today at over $3 at the port of Vancouver, it is a tragedy for western farmers that Canada effectively stopped selling wheat some seven months ago. The expenditure of $48 million for 20 miles of grain cars is pretty dramatic stuff for us in western Canada. These cars are highly visible as they move around the Prairies, painted in appropriate colours, bright orange ana gold. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, nothing like it has ever been seen on Canadian rail lines before. The only thing missing is the minister's signature.
Let me draw attention to some of the things the federal government should be doing to help the grain transportation industry. First, we should be moving away from the inner harbour of Vancouver out to Roberts Bank where there is sufficient depth of water to accommodate the new large bulk carriers, giving us lower ocean freight and where we can stockpile and where pollution will not be such a pressing problem.

Mr. Chairman, there is an alternative to the Fraser canyon route, and I think the federal government has a responsibility to act on it. It consists of a rail line some 45 miles long, joining our present CN and CP main lines just west of Kamloops to the British Columbia rail line which goes in a southwesterly direction to Squamish and Vancouver. This line would begin at Ashcroft and go up a hilly valley in a northwesterly direction to Clinton which is situated on the B.C. rail line. The proposed 45-mile loop would be built in a hilly mountain valley, not a mountainous canyon, closed-in type of terrain. At the present time there is already a highway joining these two towns.
Let me once again give the committee the figures relating to the three rail routes to the Pacific. The Prince Rupert line was blocked for five weeks last year, the Fraser canyon route was blocked for four weeks, but the proposed B.C. route was blocked for only 24 hours. Records for past years follow a similar pattern.
Our grain transportation industry has been studied to death, Mr. Chairman. In the last couple of years we have had plenty of task forces. We have had the Menzies report, a three-year transportation study which has now been passed on for another five years of study. We have had protein grading studies, quota system studies, block shipping studies and feed grain movement studies which have pitted eastern farmers against western farmers. The latest development was when the Quebec delegation walked out of the CFA meeting in Ottawa a few days ago. The government has done all these studies at great cost to the taxpayer. They have been done by very competent people who have gone as far as they can. It is now up to the government to act. What we want is some direction.
This government's response to our grain problems has been to build more and bigger bureaucracies. Let us look for a moment at some of the government organizations that the farmers and the transportation industry are expected to blueprint their way through. We have the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Grains Commission, the Canada Grains Council, the grains group in Ottawa, the Canadian (International) Grains Institute, the grains division of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Canadian government elevator system, the National Harbours Board elevator system, the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. Under growing federal government bureaucracy we now have the Manitoba Grain Commission, the Saskatchewan Grain Commission and the Alberta Grain Commission. How many more such bodies will we have to support before the government finally accepts its responsibility and moves to bring some order out of chaos?
I am apprehensive, Mr. Chairman, and so are a good many other farmers. I say this because the government
February 12, 1973

has consistently drawn the wrong conclusions, or no conclusion at all. Our grain industry has been managed by default. Three times during the last ten years we have been taken to the limit of our transportation facilities. In 1963 the Russians bought every bushel of wheat that Canada could export. In 1965 Russia and China again took all the grain we could move to export. In 1972 once again we found a desperate world at our ports and once again we were unable to accommodate the demand. Dr. Boerma, director of the Food and Agriculture Organization, has stated that world wheat stocks are now at their lowest level in 20 years, and during that period the world's population has grown by 50 per cent.
This government's action-or lack of action-is nothing short of criminal. The expenditure of $48 million on hopper cars is very difficult to justify in so far as increasing our exports of grain are concerned. Western Canadian farmers are not being saved by the politics of this government; they are being saved by the politics of hunger, by the food crisis which has made tens of millions destitute. This government must accept the blame for monumental failures in planning and implementing policies.

The hon. member made reference to the studies that have been made, and to do him credit I think he recognized that there was need to be patient until these studies made of the transportation and handling system had been completed. He criticized us for turning over the matter to the Canada Grains Council. What in fact we did was to turn it over in an effort to get the industry as a whole, and the producers in particular, to give their views as to whether or not we should move in the direction of fewer elevators and longer hauls in view of the savings that are possible.
The hon. member has been associated with the Palliser Wheat Growers Association which took a very strong stand in favour of far fewer delivery points across the prairie region, certainly a much stronger stand than I took in that direction. Indeed, they took a stronger view than that taken by the studies I have referred to, which suggested a certain degree of continued development and consolidation of delivery points. Even that view, however, means it is probable that some of the railway lines now existing will disappear, since grain was hauled along those lines to elevators which now no longer exist. Thus, these particular lines are of no further use for that purpose.
When the hon. member said that hopper cars were apt to be another thin edge of the wedge in regard to rail line
