Of course, the situation on the west coast is one in which we clearly require more storage facilities. We are all agreed on that. There is no doubt that more storage facilities are required there. I do say to the hon. member that it is not clear at all that the simple use of bulk handling facilities in that area is the answer to anything. The existing Saskatchewan wheat pool's terminal there, which is the most modern one, can handle a great deal more grain than it is now handling if it receives that grain clean. So if we can clean the grain on the Prairies, ship it to Vancouver and put it through that facility, we can handle that grain without using bulk handling facilities. I suggest this is something the wheat farmer and the wheat associations must look at very carefully before saying that bulk handling facilities are the answer.
We are told that the Kansas City review of September 13, 1972, said it was too bad that Canada was not selling grain any more because now the price has gone up so much. The Wheat Board stopped selling grain some time before the United States did because it knew the price was going up and it was waiting for it to go up. Indeed, on September 13 when the Kansas City review was saying it was too bad we were not selling grain any more, the price of grain was 30 cents or 40 cents lower than it subsequently rose to, and at that point after it had risen we sold more grain. Indeed, since that date the Canadian Wheat Board has sold 200 million bushels of wheat. That, Mr. Chairman, is the fact.
I really do not know how long we have to go on having the prairie farmers say such things as that we are out of wheat, because as at the last report I have here in my book, the amount of grain in the country three weeks ago was 1,100,000,000 bushels. We are told we have not been selling any grain. We sold 200 million bushels of wheat and we have been selling barley at a rapid rate and at a higher price, and we are continuing to sell. Those are the facts, Mr. Chairman.
We are now hearing criticism about the purchase of 2,000 hopper cars. We saw a need for the purchase of 2,000 hopper cars on the basis of the information the railways gave us. They could not assure us that in any given year, unless everything went absolutely right, they could in fact take more than about 800 million bushels of grain to destinations for export. We saw the possibility of wanting to take a good deal more than that, perhaps as much as 150 million bushels more than that for export. Hopper cars were needed to assure us that we could do that and to give us some leaway in times when markets were readily available.
We are told, again, that those hopper cars can only be operated on certain of the trackage in the prairie region. Of course that is true and it was known to us long ago when we began to look at the prairie region and the railway system there. I am not sure what the hon. member means when he says that somehow this is going to lead to more branch line abandonment. What it will lead to-and for goodness sake let us look at the positive side-is pressure on the railways to bring up their standards for the use of hopper cars on those lines which should remain in the business of grain handling. That, Mr. Chairman, is the positive side of this whole business.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks at this time which I feel are pertinent to this debate. I do not intend to become involved in statistics but will as much as possible comment generally and see that my remarks are brief.
The movement of grain on the Prairies has been a very real problem for many years. There has been a great deal of study carried out on the subject. There has been much debate, but very little action. I would suggest that the purchase of hopper cars has been the result of political expediency rather than a decision based on priority. Undoubtedly, at some time in the future hopper cars will become a priority item, but at the moment the railroads have indicated that with the rolling stock existing prior to the purchase of the cars they were able to transport approximately one billion bushels of grain annually to the west coast and Thunder Bay provided they had good weather and adequate terminal facilities.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has suggested a linking up of the CNR and CPR lines from the Kamloops area with the B.C. rail line in the Clinton area, a distance of some 45 miles. This is a rail connection that could be constructed with relative ease and at reasonable cost. This rail link, together with the improvement of facilities at Vancouver and new facilities at Roberts Bank, would save the western farmer many hundreds of thousands of dollars in demurrage. It would mean that there would be adequate supplies of export grains that would be available on site when called for by our customers. These are urgent matters.
There is the urgent matter of the port of Churchill. The port of Churchill is the nearest Atlantic ocean port to the prairie provinces. It eliminates more than 1,000 miles in comparison to the St. Lawrence Seaway route. It represents a reduction in shipping costs of from 10 cents to 15 cents per bushel. An amount of $10 million or $15 million out of the $48 million spent on hopper cars could have been spent in dredging and port rehabilitation. I suggest that such an expenditure should have had a much higher priority than hopper cars.
Supply
There is also the matter of rail line abandonment in Saskatchewan which has been delayed until 1975. The proposal of the railroads is to close down approximately 3,000 miles of the 8,500 miles of line. With the abandonment of this trackage, some 800 of the present 2,700 elevators would close down, affecting approximately 400 delivery points. The closing of these delivery points will spell the end of many of our small towns and an end to rural life, a trend which already is taking place.
I am not suggesting that there should be no rail line abandonment. What I am saying is that before any steps are taken to close down lines, the effect on small rural communities located on the lines should be seriously considered. Too often economics seem to have priority over people. Before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates we were told that something less than half the trackage in western Canada will be able to handle the new hopper cars. When considering the rail line abandonment it is imperative that we also consider rail line improvement at least into areas of high grain production.
In the past few days we have heard questions posed to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board with regard to problems of grain delivery in various areas of the Prairies. We have also heard that Canadian boxcars have been used to transport United States grain through the Prairies and out to the west coast. If Canadian cars are available to transport United States grain, why are there not cars available to clear out some of the congested delivery points on the Prairies? What are the priorities? Is the transportation of United States grain more important than the transportation of Canadian grain? Is the welfare of the United States producer more important than the welfare of the Canadian producer?
To summarize, may I say that we have reached a difficult period. Decisions must be made in the immediate future. As the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek stated, there has been a multiplicity of studies. We cannot continue having more studies. Priorities must be worked out based on statistics available from those studies and not, as I said before, based on political expediency. Unless we establish such priorities very quickly, and unless once they have been established the government carries them out, the problems will continue to be compounded and we will lose not only the developing markets but also some of our traditional markets to our more aggressive competitors.

I listened to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain make a speech that was two or three years old. I heard the hon. member for Crowfoot and the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt make the same speech, very much better, two years ago. The hon. member seemed to be attempting to revive the myth about Alvin selling wheat. I noticed the manner in which the Minister of Justice got up and after years of frustration tried to combat that myth. I believe he had some success. However, had the Minister of Justice said the kind of things he said tonight in 1969 and 1970, and had he used some muscle on the railroads what we are debating tonight might not have been necessary.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was a typical Tory when he took part in the debate, only he is a little more modern than his colleagues who spoke last week. He was marching into 1957 trying to dam the waters that have already gone under the bridge. I appreciated some of the remarks of the Minister of Justice. I even understood and sympathized with his last-ditch defence of Lift. I hope he keeps that up in my constituency. But again, Mr. Chairman, that is water under the bridge.
It is amusing to hear the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and the Minister of Justice rise back and forth for four and a half years and say to each other, "I sold more wheat than you did". Which one sold the most wheat? All this has been done at the expense of the wheat growers in the prairie provinces. Both of them talk about maximum production but they say nothing about price or, if they talk about price, they say that we have too much production. Both of them have spoken this way for many years, and while both of them have been in government we have lost tens of thousands of grain growers in the three prairie provinces.
Only the organizational genius of the old-line parties could do such a thing in a country which grows grains naturally. It is amusing to hear them talking about prices. When in mid-September the Tories promised an increase of 25 or 30 cents a bushel, the Minister of Justice pulled their teeth the next day and beat them by a nickel. What both of them forgot was that they were not fooling the farmers. It was the farmers' own money. The Minister of Justice could have announced the price to take effect at the beginning of the crop year on August 1; he could have done it in July. Of course, it made a better announcement coming in late September or October. However, he outbid the Conservatives by a nickel a bushel, using the farmers' own money.
The minister had the fortitude to mention the stabilization bill this evening and I am glad he brought up the subject. If it is his intention and the intention of his government to reintroduce that little item, I would like to refresh his memory. Perhaps he will recall that during the debate on that measure, before it was withdrawn four things were put forward which should have been included in the bill if it was to be acceptable to western grain farmers. One of them, I am happy to note, has been done; that is, having to do with crop insurance.
May I refresh the minister's memory, if he intends to bring that in again, that there are three remaining things

to do or revisions to make in his stabilization plan if it is to have any acceptance in the House or among farm organizations or grain producers in western Canada. The first is grain storage. I hope that by now the minister has given up the idea of repealing the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. We would welcome some positive amendments to it, but we hope he has given up that idea. We hope that he and his colleagues have now come around to what we put forward a year and a half ago, that the nation as a whole should bear some share of the cost of grain storage, not just on wheat but on all grains.
Second, the plan must be based on net income, not gross income. I do not need to say anything more on that subject. The minister went to the farm organizations and to the provinces, and I hope he has that message by now before he brings in any new stabilization plan. Third, the plan must be based on some kind of guaranteed price which has some relationship to the cost of production, or a combination of guaranteed prices and some control over rising farm costs. Those three things must be included before any stabilization plan becomes acceptable to grain farmers in western Canada.
We have had so-called surpluses in Canada and so-called world shortages, and successive old-line governments have played around with farm prices using the farmers' own money. Farm prices have always fluctuated at the beck and call of the so-called world markets. I submit, Sir, that until a national government is prepared to back the grain industry on prices and not leave them to the whims of world markets, we will continue to have the problems we have had in the past.
It is not good enough for either the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain or the Minister of Justice to brag about how much grain each of them moved if, first, the grain was sold at an insufficient price or, second, there was no guarantee or protection on those prices for grain producers when production is at a decent level. Surely this is part of what we have to do. We cannot leave individual grain growers at the mercy of what happens on the world markets. It requires the strength and wealth of the entire nation to support agricultural prices and, in this instance, grain prices.
Earlier tonight mention was made of orderly marketing, which I find most amusing coming from members of the Liberal and Tory parties who have talked a good fight on that subject for all these years. I would say to the Minister of Justice that we in this party support, and always have since the inception of our party in 1932, the orderly marketing of all six grains under the Canadian Wheat Board. In fact, there were only five grains in those years. We still support that.
I accept the idea of a plebiscite. I am confident that the overwhelming majority of grain growers in western Canada want the three grains to be under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. I am confident that rape-seed growers are sick and tired of the kind of pricing that has been imposed on them. It is all very well for the minister to lie back and rely on a plebiscite. I wonder, however, if his heart is really in it. What action is he personally taking, and what action is the Canadian Wheat Board and the government taking to provide the kind of positive information to grain growers that will lead them

to unanimously want to include rapeseed under the Canadian Wheat Board?
I am afraid what will be allowed to happen is that fast buck operators from grain exchanges and free enterprises will ride the backs of grain growers and start another propaganda war trying to undermine, undercut and destroy the whole principle of orderly marketing through a public, producer-controlled board. It is not good enough to say that we are all for a plebiscite. It will require some leadership. We submit that it will require leadership from members of all parties in the House if we are to enlarge and enhance the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board for the benefit of the grain growers, and this applies to feed grains as well as to the board's grains.
Unless and until this happens, the kind of things that have been happening to rapeseed prices and to flax and rye prices will be happening, that is, that they will have no relationship to the value and worth of the product. They have only related to what the speculators could make on them, with no relationship to the real value and worth of the product or to what it cost to raise and produce, and little or no relationship to what the farmer needed to have left over for himself. I submit that not until these grains are under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board will we get some fair, reasonable and decent pricing on these three grains.
I would like to hear where the Conservative party stands on this. I would like to hear from all the prairie cowboys whether or not they are in favour of flax, rye and rapeseed being under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. I would be interested to know, because I can assure them that whichever way they say they would prefer it, I would be happy to circulate every speech in my riding and in other parts of the Prairies.
We would like to know, are you or are you not in favour of those grains being under the Canadian Wheat Board? We would like to know if the Minister of Justice is in favour or not. And if there are any other Liberals from the three prairie provinces, we would like to know their position. There is one from Winnipeg. We would like to know whether he is in favour or not. An answer from him should be a dandy. We would like the Minister of National Defence to tell us whether or not he is in favour of these three grains being under the Canadian Wheat Board.
The Minister of Agriculture may or may not have expressed himself on this matter, but we would like to hear from him as well. We would like to know whether or not he is in favour of these three grains being under the Canadian Wheat Board. If nothing else, we would like to know his own personal opinion. I give him credit for that, Mr. Chairman; he is not afraid to express his personal opinion. He has given such opinions in the past. Is he for or against these three grains being under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board? If these three gentlemen express positive personal opinions they will provide some kind of responsible leadership and help the grain growers of western Canada.
I also hope that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board will arrange for a lot of information to be given to grain producers very quickly, to support a plebiscite on
Supply
the question of bringing these three grains under the Canadian Wheat Board. I hope he is not merely playing around and could not care less whether the plebiscite wins or loses in that respect. I also hope that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board will be present when we get to the vote in the estimates dealing with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce because we have some questions to ask him concerning hopper cars. I will not go into that subject very much tonight, although others have raised it.
But when it comes to the matter of rail line abandonment, Mr. Chairman, we for one group expect that the minister and the government will either formally make representations to the Canadian Transport Commission or, if necessary, overrule the commission and, as a minimum, place a five-year moratorium on any further rail line abandonment. Anything less than that will be a betrayal of grain growers and of hundreds of towns and villages in western Canada. Just to illustrate, I mention one line in my constituency which connects the villages and towns on Dilke, Holdfast, Penzance, Liberty, Stalwart, Simpson, and Imperial, some 130 miles of track slated to go if the CPR can get its way. The minister talks about a 5 cents a bushel saving from abandonment. I would like him to tell us whether that 5 cents a bushel saving is just for the CPR and the grain companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext: For the farmers.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)
speechtext:
If that is for the farmers, I would like the minister to explain what will be done when grain is hauled great distances in trucks carrying 1,000 to 1,500 bushels, along municipal road systems not one mile of which is capable of carrying those loads? What will that mean in land taxes to farmers? I repeat, where does the 5 cents a bushel go? Is it still a 5 cents a bushel saving to farmers if, in addition to hauling their wheat a distance two or three times greater than before, they have to travel that farther distance to buy their groceries and farm implements?
What happens if these towns and villages become ghost towns and villages? Add up the cost if these scores of towns and villages with their streets, sidewalks, churches, schools, curling rinks, elevators, and other community services are abandoned, not to mention the grocery stores and implement dealerships. Is the minister going to ask all those people to get up and walk away from their communities? Surely not.
I want to see a lot more information before the minister can convince me or anybody else on the Colonsay subdivision of the CPR, that its abandonment will mean a saving of 5 cents a bushel. But even if by some stretch of the imagination or statistics-bending that was correct, has anybody added up the social and human costs involved? Are they included in that 5 cents a bushel? What is going to happen to those communities? The debenture debt is not even paid on the sewer, water and road systems. Surely the minimum we must have is for the government either to request the CTC or overrule the CTC, so that there will be a minimum moratorium of five years past 1975 on any rail line abandonment. That is the minimum time that will be needed in order to find out all we need to know before one more mile of track is lifted.

Adjournment Debate

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I really enjoyed what might be called the Saskatchewan debate this evening. I think all the speakers were from that province. It was interesting to see the Minister of Justice rise time and again and make accolades to himself. This is one of the disadvantages of coming back alone to parliament; you don't have anyone else to blow your horn so you must blow it yourself. We heard the debate between the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and the former minister. We are not really able to judge who won tonight. But the same debate was carried on in Saskatchewan last October and I will accept the judgment of the people of that province; they were in the best position to know.
I take exception to the minister's comments about the Conservative party. It is rather discouraging to have the king of the grain bootleggers make criticisms like that. I say that his pet answer as to why Lift was introduced was utter nonsense. He said it was to clean out the system. He decreased the amount of grain in the system by 200 million bushels. He forced that amount of grain to be stored again on the farms for one reason and one reason only, to reduce the amount which the treasury had to pay under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. There is no way he will get me to believe anything different.
Perhaps this great salesman would rise at the close of my remarks tomorrow and tell us about the barley payment on last year's crop. And what about the final wheat payment? It was rumoured that it would be paid out on February 1, and then on February 12 which is today. I suppose now it will be paid on Friday. Maybe the politicians over there are still trying to steal a little out of this year's pool to make it look good politically?
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE PENSIONS- INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE INCREASE-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE PENSIONS- INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE INCREASE-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 24 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) if he intended to present at an early date legislation to provide the promised substantial increase in old age security pensions. The minister replied that he had scheduled yet another dominion-provincial conference and that such a meeting was to be held on February 2. The minister announced that the discussions with his provincial counterparts were "consultations" and that he envisaged no veto power for any or all of the provinces.

It is difficult to understand, let alone appreciate, what the government intends in this most important sector of the social welfare field. The Speech from the Throne declared, "a reconsideration of Canada's social security system must be conducted jointly by the federal government and the provinces". Later, the same document promises, nevertheless, "legislation will be introduced to improve the economic situation of the old age pensioners". The Speech from the Throne has been adopted, the minister has had a conference, he has promised more than once a substantial increase in the old age pension- but where is the legislation? If it were -needed at the time of the drafting of the Speech from the Throne, how much greater is the need now as prices continue to soar and the purchasing power of the old age security cheque shrinks with painful inevitability under this government's inflationary economy.
Two eminent economists, one from the Canada Council on Social Development and one from the Department of Urban Affairs recently indicated that about 50 per cent of Canadians over 65 years of age were living in poverty. Over 50 per cent, Mr. Speaker. What a situation! What a condition in a country with such potential for prosperity as Canada to have one-half the senior citizens having to eke out an existence at or near the poverty line.
It is time to bring on some measure of relief, some measure of justice for those who receive the old age security pension, now possessed of ever-diminishing purchasing power. I assured the minister and the House the other day that if he abandons his immobility on the matter and brings down the legislation we will assist him get it into the hands of the old age pensioners where it has belonged for lo these many months. How wrong it is to think, Mr. Speaker, that just because these people do not qualify for the supplement, do not in fact pass the means test, they are therefore affluent and are living a luxurious life, when indeed many of them are on the very edge of painful poverty.
My colleague from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) was telling me a moment ago about being in a supermarket in Ottawa this morning when he saw an old age pensioner look at a jar of honey, put it in the cart, calculate again what his pension was and then put the jar back on the shelf.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE PENSIONS- INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE INCREASE-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE PENSIONS- INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE INCREASE-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: These people are in dire straits. They need help, and they need it now. Mr. Speaker, there is no reason for delay. Surely, on the contrary, there are compelling economic reasons for action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE PENSIONS- INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE INCREASE-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question raised by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) on January 24, I should point out that on January 11 the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) indicated quite clearly what the government had in mind in respect of increases for old age pensioners. He indicated that consultation was taking place with provincial ministers of health and that further consultations would take place. He made an
February 12, 1973

unequivocal statement that substantial increases in the old age pension would be forthcoming.
On January 24 the hon. member for Hillsborough indicated that he was in a bit of a quandary on this subject. He did not seem to know why we would consult on the matter when in fact we had already made up our minds that there would be a substantial increase. I should like to point out to him that consultation does not mean that they who are being consulted will make the final decision on what will be done. The fact of the matter is that this kind of consultation means that the Department of National Health and Welfare is concerned with the view of the provincial ministers and would like to take them into account in its deliberations. However, that does not preclude the possibility of achieving the objective of the government's statement to provide substantial increases. It could be increased in terms of the old age pension itself, the OAS, the GIS or a combination of both.
It is quite important to the government to know the views of the provincial ministers of welfare in this respect prior to introducing legislation in this House. The minister indicated that that legislation will be coming down very shortly. I think all members of this House will agree that when that legislation is presented it will do something very worth while for all the old age pensioners in Canada.

subtopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-MEASURES TO ACCELERATE APPROVAL OF PROJECTS
MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-MEASURES TO ACCELERATE APPROVAL OF PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raised the question of the insufficient funds made available to the Department of Manpower and Immigration for its Local Initiatives Program by asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when additional credits would be made available to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) to enable him to approve a greater number of projects with a view to creating jobs and settling some of the problems facing the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
In his reply the minister stated that he would take the suggestions into account.
During the previous program, namely the 1971-72 program, 38 per cent of the projects submitted were approved and implemented. As a rule, the results were satisfactory.
When this program was renewed for 1972-73, the minister stated that it met the needs of the rural population as well as those of the urban population and that it permitted a direct and rapid intervention in high unemployment regions and often made it possible to create new kinds of employment. The minister also said that this program would permit the implementation of projects which the people themselves consider essential for their collectivity but which could not be implemented before.
The government saw fit to renew this program this year and, as a representative of the people, it was my duty to inform my constituents and to invite them to submit projects.
Adjournment Debate
The Canadian population responded to the government in such a way that over 16,000 projects have been submitted. Unfortunately, for lack of funds, less than one third have been approved to date.
If the government is truly sincere and willing to fight unemployment it should at least double the funds earmarked for this purpose.
In the second place, it is high time for the government to state frankly what criteria are applied for approval of projects. It is increasingly difficult for a member of Parliament to ascertain the true facts in this respect. Moreover, the public is concerned about allegations that patronage-minded Liberals are imposing their views on selection of projects emanating from ridings represented by non-Liberal members. I hope there is no truth in such rumours, but it is time to give the public frank reassurances in this respect.
The minister has already stated that the main consideration for acceptance of a project is the level of unemployment in the locality from which it originates, which is reasonable.
If such is the case, I suggest that it would be equitable for more projects to be approved in Eastern Quebec, some of them in the riding of Bellechasse which has been sadly neglected for many years, long before I became its representative and where there are major economic and social needs to be met.
That is why I am insisting on approval and implementation of a greater number of projects as early as possible, in order to provide employment for a greater number of workers and to reduce the number of people now forced on welfare.
The minister has instructed his officials to send to all hon. members copies of projects submitted and originating from their respective ridings, accompanied by a letter asking for each hon. member's comments, if any are warranted. This is a most generous gesture on the part of the minister. It will enable hon. members to acquaint themselves with each one of the projects and judge whether or not they will meet the needs of the locality.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to another point which is most troubling, that is, to the announcement of the Quebec minister for municipal affairs to the effect that he accepted such and such a program.
This news published in the newspapers lead the public to believe far more projects are adopted than are in fact. If the reader is the least bit careful, he will discover that the good news of the minister is conditional on the projects being accepted at the federal level because the federal government pays.
In the final analysis, it is just a matter of partisan propaganda of which the public has long since had its fill. This does nothing to help create jobs for the unemployed or to implement projects.
So I ask once more that additional credits be voted for this program, that the project examination and approval procedure be accelerated and that consideration be given to recommendations by Manpower Centres and the organizations concerned, which are more qualified than anyone else to inform adequately the officials responsible for

February 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
making final decisions. This is urgent; the unemployed cannot wait any longer.
I hope very much that we shall receive a favourable reply and that the projects will be approved in greater numbers and implemented in the best interest of working people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question originally raised by the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Lambert) had to do with the speed of processing LIP applications. The minister has on several occasions this year responded to similar questions. On January 8, as reported at page 40 of Hansard, he said the following:
I cannot give a precise date but in all sincerity it will be done just as quickly as it can be done wisely.
That might be said to be the principle upon which we have been proceeding with respect to the processing of LIP applications. This evening the hon. member has raised several other questions including, principally, that of the sufficiency of the fund. It should be pointed out that the regular LIP fund has in fact been exhausted since January 19, and to the extent that the LIP fund has been kept open since that date this has been possible as a result of the transfer of funds from the on-the-job training program and from the business LIP.
The minister suggested to the hon. member in his answer on February 6 that he thought it likely that $10 million would be transferred from the on-the-job program to LIP but, as a matter of fact, only $5 million has been transferred because there was a considerable upswing in applications for on-the-job training during the last week of the application period and it will be possible to put people to work under this program at a faster rate than the minister had anticipated when he answered on February 6.
With respect to the $10 million set aside for business LIP, $7 million has been transferred back to regular LIP. It is anticipated that only $1 million will be required for fund projects approved under the business LIP segment of the program although, of course, these projects will serve as a valuable tool for assessing the viability of the particular program involved.
To bring the House up to date I should like to give the latest available figures on the Local Initiatives Program, taken from the computer as of Friday, February 9. The applications received numbered 15,269; the dollar value of these applications was $487, 121,698. The number of applications approved was 5,732; the dollar value of the applications approved was $162.6 million. Man-months of employment created, 332,732.
Unofficially, as of this time, all available funds have been committed to approved projects. The official figures from the computer will be available tomorrow or Wednesday. It may be the case that there will be some further small transfers of funds. subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE-STEPS TO ENSURE ADEQUATE NUMBER OF PLANES AND VESSELS FOR ACCIDENTS OFF EAST COAST

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE-STEPS TO ENSURE ADEQUATE NUMBER OF PLANES AND VESSELS FOR ACCIDENTS OFF EAST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 26, as reported at page 683 of Hansard, I directed a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson). I asked the minister what steps he was taking to ensure adequate search and rescue capabilities off the east coast of Canada, in view of the serious incident that took place recently when it took ten hours to evacuate the crew of a stranded Canadian trawler only a very short distance from the coast of Newfoundland because there were no helicopters based there. The minister replied that the government was looking at the possibility of decentralizing it-that is, the search and rescue facilities-somewhat and increasing our capability in Newfoundland. That is more or less a direct quotation.
My question was prompted by the grounding of the Newfoundland trawler Cape Brule in heavy seas off the south coast of Newfoundland early in January of this year. Because of the heavy seas in the area at the time, the vessel was in great danger of breaking up, placing the lives of the 14 crew members in imminent danger. The nearest search and rescue aircraft are stationed in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, some considerable distance to the west. Consequently, it took ten hours to get the Canadian forces search and rescue helicopter to the scene to evacuate the crew.
This is not the first such incident, Mr. Speaker, and it is unfortunate that the limited time at my disposal does not permit me to go into the others. There was a search and rescue unit based in St. John's up to 1963, when it was moved to Greenwood, Nova Scotia, some 500 miles to the west. The situation has been further aggravated by the departure of the U.S. Coastguard from Argentia, Newfoundland.
The situation concerning the grounding of the Cape Brule and the lack of air/sea search and rescue capability in the area was summed up by the St. John's Evening Telegram in an editorial on January 18, 1973. The editorial is headed "Ottawa needs a map", and I shall quote part of it:
Has anybody in Canada got a map of Newfoundland? We doubt it, for anybody with such a map and the sense that God gave to a broody hen would see right off that Newfoundland is the obvious place in which to locate air and sea rescue operations. It has a long and dangerous coastline, it is close to the major Atlantic shipping routes, it sits astride the main fishing areas and it has five fully fledged airports, as well as a number of suitable airstrips.
The editorial goes on to say:
It is only too obvious that aircraft could have been on the scene within an hour if Argentia, Gander or St. John's had rescue aircraft ready to move at short notice.
On January 24, 1973, I wrote to the Minister of National Defence outlining the urgency of the situation and the need for immediate remedial action. I realize, of course, that the minister has been preoccupied of late with the Viet Nam situation, but I do not think it is overstating the

case to say that unless the government acts, and acts soon, we are going to be faced with a serious marine disaster.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) has already announced that four specially designed lifeboats will be built and placed into service by the Department of Transport. Surely the Department of National Defence, which is currently in the process of redefining the role of the Canadian armed forces, has to bear a great deal of the responsibility since it has aircraft at its disposal plus the experience to co-ordinate and carry out successfully an air/sea rescue operation.
My province, which has a coastline of 6,000 miles, is involved in year-round deep sea fishing operations. God knows, fishing is a hazardous occupation at the best of times but is particularly dangerous in the wintertime. The province of Newfoundland, particularly the east coast, should be the logical site for an air/sea rescue unit. Thanks to the United States, there are adequate and excellent base facilities available. An aircraft stationed in eastern Newfoundland would add almost a thousand miles to their capability and would reduce substantially the time it would take to deploy a helicopter to a stricken vessel.
In addition, I think it is also fair to say, for the record, that the province of Newfoundland has been shortchanged in so far as national defence spending is concerned. We do not have a major Canadian forces base in the province of Newfoundland, apart from a very small communications unit stationed at Gander and a very small unit based in Goose Bay, Labrador, which is there mainly to assist the huge U.S. base located there.
I believe this would be an excellent opportunity for the government to correct that situation and to provide the province of Newfoundland with an air/sea search and rescue unit which would serve to protect the many thousands of Canadian fishermen who fish off the coast of Newfoundland and, more particularly-I underline this because I think it is urgent this winter when we are experiencing severe ice conditions-it would serve in my view to avert a very major marine disaster. I believe it is incumbent upon the government to act immediately because of the seriousness of the situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE-STEPS TO ENSURE ADEQUATE NUMBER OF PLANES AND VESSELS FOR ACCIDENTS OFF EAST COAST
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I
Adjournment Debate
should like to compliment the hon. member for bringing forward this subject of search and rescue as it pertains to the Canadian armed forces, because they have had an excellent record over the years. In this very serious task we do run into many difficulties.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has expressed his very real concern on the subject of search and rescue to the minister in private discussions, by letter, by question in the House and during this debate tonight. I wish to advise him that the minister also has a very real interest in the search and rescue capability of the department.
I believe the hon. member is aware that the Department of National Defence is, by cabinet direction, responsible for providing search and rescue facilities capable of responding to air distress incidents in accordance with Canada's international responsibilities as agreed with the International Civil Aviation Association and also in terms of our own domestic requirements. Providing resources to deal with marine distress incidents is primarily the responsibility of the ministry of transport. I understand that department will shortly be commissioning four new lifeboats, as the hon. member mentioned, for use in the Newfoundland area.
I know the hon. member does appreciate, however, that when there is a distress call, be it air or marine, the search and rescue facilities of the Canadian forces are immediately alerted and provide whatever assistance is possible. The Canadian forces do, through the rescue co-ordination centres, provide co-ordinating services for both air and marine incidents.
In the specific rescue operation involving the motor vessel Cape Brule to which the hon. member has referred, I should like to point out that from the first indication that the ship was in distress until a search and rescue aircraft was over the Cape Brule, was 5 j hours, not 10 hours as the hon. member indicated in his question on January 26.
Furthermore, from the time it became apparent that a helicopter was required to effect a rescue of the crew members until the search and rescue helicopter was taking the first survivors from the Cape Brule, was 4 hours and 21 minutes. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does have the minister's assurance that he is looking at the possibility of some decentralization of the search and rescue capability.

Tuesday. February 13, 1973
